clue.text: Last words when writing to accept the part?

definitions.text: Last words when writing to accept the part?

parts.words: Last words when writing to accept the part?
parts.note: an afterthought added below a signature reads like a whimsical reply sent by an actor taking a role, posting back the play's text

explanation.surface: An actor writes a letter accepting a role and wonders how to sign off.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the plain sense: words added at the end of a letter. The question mark covers the playful second reading, of an actor accepting a part by putting the play's text in the mail.
explanation.definitionFit: The note added after a letter's signature is the final thing written, so it is literally the last words.

clue.text: Bear's disdainful expression

definitions.meaning: Winnie-the-... is A. A. Milne's bear; 's stands for 'is'

explanation.definitionFit: Milne's famous teddy bear shares his name with a scoffing exclamation of contempt.

clue.text: Less than a foot bridge

definitions.meaning: an old measure of nine inches, the stretch of a spread hand
the arch or stretch between supports of a bridge

explanation.definitionFit: The handspan measure was nine inches, under a foot, and the same word names the arch that crosses a gap.

clue.text: Her torn pages embarrassed the dictator's aide

indicators.note: the torn pages are thrown into disorder, as embarrassed once meant confused, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A secretary's notebook is ripped and she is mortified in front of her boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embarrassed' is the anagram signal on HER TORN PAGES. The 'dictator' is someone dictating letters, not a tyrant.
explanation.definitionFit: A shorthand typist takes down what someone dictates, so assists the person dictating.

clue.text: In a Paris street, a church gathering

indicators.note: In places the church inside the French street, as a building stands within a road

parts.note: rue is French for street

explanation.surface: A congregation meets in a church on a Parisian street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gathering' looks like a congregation, but it is a dressmaking term: a gathered frill.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruche is a frill of fabric gathered up in pleats, a dressmaking gather.

clue.text: The last of the soap when the first has gone

definitions.text: The last of the soap when the first has gone

parts.words: The last of the soap when the first has gone
parts.note: take the opening letter from the word soap and what is left is the abbreviation for an old-age retiree

explanation.surface: Talking about the final sliver of a cake of soap.
explanation.walkthrough: SOAP without its first letter is OAP, Old Age Pensioner, a British term for a retired person on a state pension.
explanation.definitionFit: OAP abbreviates old-age pensioner, a person receiving a state pension after retirement.

clue.text: Card experts

definitions.meaning: the top-ranking card of each suit
people who excel at something, champions

explanation.definitionFit: The highest playing card in a suit shares its name with people who are outstanding at a skill.

clue.text: Pacify with nice coat, new style, about £1

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the shuffled letters go round the money piece
the coat's words are given a fresh look, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: L, from Latin libra, is the pound sign
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Calming someone down by buying them a nice new-style coat for a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new style' makes CONCIATE from NICE COAT; 'about' puts it around L and I (£1).
explanation.definitionFit: To win over or soothe an angry person is to placate them.

clue.text: A way to get up, having slept badly over Summer

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second
having slept badly suggests the letters are disturbed and must be rearranged

parts.note: someone who adds up figures is an adder

explanation.surface: Someone who had a restless night finds a way to get out of bed in summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' turns SLEPT into STEPL, which sits 'over' ADDER. 'Summer' means one who sums, not the season.
explanation.definitionFit: Folding steps are a device for climbing to a height, a means of going upward.

clue.text: For colour-changing place stone in new position

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are set out in a new order, as a stone is moved to a new spot

explanation.surface: Advice to a jeweller: reset the gem to show off its shifting colours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in new position' is the anagram signal on PLACE STONE; 'For' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something showing a milky play of shifting hues, like an opal, changes colour as you look at it.

clue.text: But children's stories often start thus

definitions.text: But children's stories often start thus

parts.words: But children's stories often start thus
parts.note: the word that opens the stock fairy-tale beginning about a long-ago time; the 'But' hints at the alternative sense of 'formerly'

explanation.surface: A remark on how nursery tales tend to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: Fairy tales classically open with the formula 'upon a time', preceded by this word; the clue just describes that habit.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional opening of fairy tales is 'upon a time' preceded by this single word meaning formerly.

clue.text: In which optimists appear grateful

parts.note: the grace 'For what we are about to receive, may the Lord make us truly thankful' gives thanks in advance

explanation.surface: Describing a mood in which hopeful people seem thankful.
explanation.walkthrough: Optimists look forward to good things; the grace before meals thanks God for food not yet received, i.e. gratitude in advance.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking ahead hopefully is expectancy, the state in which one is thankful in advance.

clue.text: Mimi's role in another opera?

definitions.meaning: Mimi is the heroine of Puccini's La Boheme, a young woman of the artists' Latin Quarter
Balfe's 1843 opera about a gypsy girl carries this title

explanation.definitionFit: Mimi plays a young woman of Bohemian Paris, and Michael Balfe wrote an English opera of exactly that title.

clue.text: Had an example of one that's past

definitions.text: Had an example of one that's past

parts.words: Had an example of one that's past
parts.note: the word 'had' is the past form of the verb 'have' used with auxiliaries, a grammatical example

explanation.surface: Someone recalls having once seen a specimen of something long gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had' is the past participle of 'have'; read as grammar, the clue says 'had' is an example of a past one.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatically, 'had' is a verb form used after 'have', the kind called past participle.

clue.text: Getting the army to take in 1,000 under canvas

indicators.note: under canvas means sheltered by it, so these pieces sit inside the canvas piece

parts.note: a canvas here is taken as a tent, the shelter troops sleep in
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve
taken as written
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Arranging for the army to put up a thousand soldiers in tents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under' puts TA, IN and M inside A TENT; 'to take' is a link. The parse reads 'canvas' loosely as 'a tent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Achievement or acquisition is the act of obtaining something, a noun sense of getting.

clue.text: Always, apparently, time for lotos-eating

parts.note: Tennyson's poem The Lotos-Eaters describes a land in which it seemed always a certain part of the day

explanation.surface: A lazy land where it is permanently the hour for idling.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's The Lotos-Eaters: 'In the afternoon they came unto a land / In which it seemed always afternoon.' The lotos-eaters of Homer drift in drugged idleness.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's lotos-eaters reach a land where the post-lunch hours seem never to end, so that drowsy period is their eternal time.

clue.text: Top jobs-odd noises show the idea persists

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, so jobs loses its opening letter
odd noises are strange ones, so the letters of noises are rearranged

explanation.surface: A peculiar racket in the workplace keeps preying on someone's mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' strips J from JOBS, giving OBS; 'odd' turns NOISES into ESSION. 'show' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixation is a thought that keeps returning and will not leave the mind.

clue.text: Investors' Chronicle — all Greek to us

definitions.text: Investors' Chronicle — all Greek to us

parts.words: Investors' Chronicle — all Greek to us
parts.note: to invest a city is to besiege it, so the investors are the besiegers of Troy, and their chronicle is a Greek epic

explanation.surface: A financial weekly whose jargon is incomprehensible to ordinary readers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Investors Chronicle is a real British financial magazine; here 'invest' means lay siege to, and the epic of the siege of Troy is literally in Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's epic narrates the Greek siege of Troy, so it is the record of the besiegers, written in Greek.

clue.text: But Kipling's lady wasn't one

parts.note: the song 'The Lady Is a ...' says one lady is a vagrant; the clue says a lady in Kipling was not

explanation.surface: A defence of a literary heroine's respectability.
explanation.walkthrough: Rodgers and Hart's song is 'The Lady Is a Tramp'; the clue contrasts that with a lady in Kipling. A tramp is also a cargo ship, and Kipling wrote much about ships.
explanation.definitionFit: A vagrant who wanders without a home is the type the famous song calls its lady, unlike Kipling's.

clue.text: Ever set it incorrectly by your plate?

indicators.note: setting the letters wrongly signals they must be rearranged, as a badly laid table is reset

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a napkin was laid in the wrong place at the dinner table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incorrectly' is the anagram signal on EVER SET IT. The definition is a descriptive one, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A table napkin is laid beside each diner's place setting, so it is found next to your plate.

clue.text: Church recess for King Edward?

definitions.meaning: a booth in a church where a priest hears sins
Edward the Confessor, English king before the Norman Conquest, so the adjective describes him

explanation.definitionFit: A booth where penitents admit their sins sits in a church, and the word also jokingly means suited to Edward the Confessor.

clue.text: Fantastic? Not in the boundaries of Rome

parts.note: out is the opposite of in

indicators.note: the boundaries are the first and last letters of the word Rome

explanation.surface: Wondering whether it is fantastic to be outside the city limits of Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the boundaries of' takes R and E, the first and last letters of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Outre, borrowed from French, means bizarre or eccentric, beyond the bounds of convention.

clue.text: Where islanders make hot drinks

definitions.meaning: a Hebridean island off the Scottish west coast
to heat wine or ale with spices

explanation.definitionFit: Mull is an island in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland, and to mull wine is to warm it with spices.

clue.text: Paper to show my understanding of French

indicators.note: in a down clue standing under means placed below the other piece

parts.note: de is the French word for 'of'

explanation.surface: A paper written to demonstrate how well I understand French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'understanding' is split as 'under-standing': MY goes below DE in the down entry. 'to show' is a link; 'of French' means the French for 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Demy is a traditional size of printing and writing sheet, so it names a kind of paper.

clue.text: Look! The Little dog's turned tail!

indicators.note: the tail end of the dog's word is turned round, so only the final pair of letters swap

parts.note: a peke is a Pekingese, a small dog

explanation.surface: A startled cry as a small dog flees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned tail' reverses only the tail of PEKE, its last two letters KE, giving EK.
explanation.definitionFit: To glance quickly or slyly is a synonym for having a look.

clue.text: Hand out what an Ephesian goddess paid to Caesar?

parts.note: Diana of the Ephesians, shortened to Di, with the possessive 's
tribute is what subjects paid to Caesar

explanation.surface: Wondering what a pagan goddess owed the Roman emperor in tax.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as DI'S TRIBUTE: Diana of Ephesus (from Acts 19) gives DI, and 'Render unto Caesar' supplies the tribute; 'what' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To dole out or share among several people is to distribute.

clue.text: Herein the best example of an Italian house

indicators.note: Herein says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Promoting a building as the finest specimen of Italian domestic architecture.
explanation.walkthrough: The House of Este was the ducal family of Ferrara and Modena; 'house' means dynasty, not building.
explanation.definitionFit: The Este family were a ruling dynasty of Ferrara and Modena, an Italian noble line.

clue.text: US hospital doctor meets friend inside

parts.note: an intern is a junior doctor in an American hospital
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: A junior American doctor runs into a friend indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening within the body or an organisation happens on the inside.
